newsitem.title: USA: Air standards fight puts clean air law at risk.
newsitem.headline: Air standards fight puts clean air law at risk.

text.p: Industry groups are likely to press for changes in the Clean Air Act if the Clinton administration approves a controversial plan to tighten air quality standards, an oil industry official said Thursday.

"I would predict that if the EPA made substantial changes ... it would cause the Clean Air Act to be reopened," said Paul Bailey, director of health and environmental affairs at the American Petroleum Institute.
EPA is expected to issue a proposal by November 29 calling for stricter standards for smog-forming emissions and fine particles.

Industry groups estimate that more than 150 counties around the United States, which currently meet ozone or fine particle pollution standards, would exceed the more stringent limits, and would have to take steps to curb emissions from cars, utilities, manufacturing plants and other sources.
About 60 counties currently do not meet one or both of the existing standards.

"If we end up with a lot more 'non-attainment' areas under either new standard, it is my judgment politically there will be a compelling reason for reopening the Clean Air Act," Bailey said at a DC Bar Association luncheon.

Several House lawmakers in the Republican-led Congress over the last two years sought to amend the Clean Air Act, including House Majority Whip Tom DeLay, R-Texas, who called for repealing the 1990 law, but the proposals did not go far.
"The threat has been out there. I'm sure it will continue to be in the next Congress," said Deborah Shprentz of the Natural Resources Defense Council.
NRDC is one of several groups pushing for strong new air quality rules which health advocates say would improve the health of millions.
